# P0304 Code on PT Cruiser: Diagnosing Cylinder 4 Oil Leaks

A P0304 code indicates a misfire specifically in cylinder number 4. On a 2005 PT Cruiser Convertible, this symptom combined with an active oil leak in the same cylinder suggests a mechanical failure that has likely compromised the combustion seal or cooled components. You have already addressed the most common external causes: the valve cover gasket and tube seals are replaced, spark plugs and wires are new, and the ignition coil is functional. Furthermore, the PCV system checks out, and a compression test returned a healthy 120 psi across all cylinders, including cylinder 4.

This specific combination of symptomsâa localized oil leak in cylinder 4 triggering a P0304 despite good compression and fresh ignition componentsâpoints toward an internal issue within the head assembly or the valve train mechanics rather than a simple seal failure. The oil leak is likely the root cause of the misfire, not just a side effect. Oil dripping onto the hot exhaust port of cylinder 4 can create immediate misfires due to carbon buildup or direct quenching of the spark plug tip before ignition occurs. However, since you have already replaced the valve cover gasket and tube seals without resolving the leak, the source is likely deeper within the engine block or head.

Consider the possibility of a cracked cylinder head or a blown head gasket localized to cylinder 4. While compression tests often yield acceptable readings if the crack is small or located in a way that doesn't significantly affect peak cylinder pressure during the power stroke, oil can still seep through these micro-fractures or into the combustion chamber via the exhaust valve guide seals. In PT Cruisers of this era, the aluminum head is prone to thermal cracking under stress. If oil is actively dripping onto the spark plug well from an internal source above the valve cover (such as a cracked rocker arm stud seal or a failed intake manifold gasket directly above cylinder 4), the fresh oil will bypass your new tube seals and continue to contaminate the new spark plugs immediately after installation.

Another critical area to investigate is the exhaust valve guide seals. Even with good compression, if the guide seals are worn or damaged by heat cycles, oil can be drawn up into the combustion chamber during the intake stroke or leak down the side of the valve. This creates a rich fuel mixture and fouls the spark plug, leading to a P0304 code. The fact that compression is 120 psi does not rule this out; it only confirms that the piston rings and head gasket are largely sealing air effectively at high pressure. It does not account for liquid oil entering the cylinder during the intake phase.

To isolate the issue, remove the new spark plug from cylinder 4 immediately upon noticing the code or after a short drive. Inspect the tip for heavy wetness versus dry carbon deposits. If the plug is soaked in oil despite having a new ignition coil and wires, the leak path is likely coming from above the valve cover gasket but below the intake manifold, or it is an internal head crack allowing oil from the gallery to enter.

If visual inspection of the exhaust port and spark plug well shows oil pooling that cannot be stopped by resealing the valve cover, you may need to remove the cylinder head for a thorough inspection. Look for hairline cracks around the cylinder 4 exhaust port or valve seat area. Sometimes, the coolant crossover hose near the intake manifold can also leak internally into the intake tract, but given the oil-specific leak, focus on the lubrication system's path into the combustion chamber.

Replacing the head gasket is often a necessary step if the crack extends into the gasket mating surface or if there is evidence of coolant mixing with oil in that specific cylinder. However, verify this by checking for bubbling in the coolant reservoir while the engine runs; if you see bubbles specifically associated with cylinder 4 issues, the head seal is compromised. Until the physical leak path is sealed from the inside out, any new seals installed on the outside will simply be overwhelmed by the volume of oil escaping from within the engine architecture.
